The Period of the Rise of Islam
But after quoting these frightening verses, the writer adds:
The Period of the Rise of Islam

“...They did not know resurrection, and they did not accept what they heard about it. None of them imagined that he would be rewarded or punished for the deeds of this life after leaving it. Their fear of the future concerned this life. They feared illness, loss of wealth and children, and loss of standing and prestige (...). As for reward after death, resurrection on the day when the trumpet is blown, Paradise prepared for the righteous, and Hell prepared for the unjust—none of this entered their minds...”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Dr. Haykal clearly falls into a contradiction here.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
On the one hand, he speaks of “their fear of resurrection and of the punishment of Hell on the Day of Judgment.” On the other, he says that they did not know resurrection and did not accept the idea.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Even so, he reaches the heart of the matter when he identifies what actually frightened the leaders of Quraysh.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
As he says, their fear of the future concerned this life.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
They feared illness, loss of wealth and children, and loss of status and prestige.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

In other words, they feared for their material interests and for the privileges they had gained through a long history of commercial, political, and religious control over the central institutions of Mecca.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
On the other side, the deprived groups of Mecca had fears of their own.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

They feared that postponing reward and punishment until the Day of Judgment would also mean postponing the solution to their own problem: the material suffering they faced under the absolute power of usury and monopoly.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Their fear too was ultimately “of the future in this life.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That, here as well, is the real issue.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

If this is the heart of the matter—and Muruwwa argues that it is—then the main factor determining the position of the two sides in the central social conflict of Meccan society was not whether they knew about resurrection or did not know about it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It is correct to discuss the matter at the level of consciousness.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The negative reactions that shaped the attitude of the Quraysh merchant aristocracy toward Islam throughout the thirteen years before the great migration to Medina were an early and undeveloped form of class consciousness.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The initial Islamic call produced a shock. It demanded the complete rejection of idols and insisted that religious belief be directed entirely toward the one and only God. At the same time, it openly mocked the idols the Meccans worshipped and condemned their worship without compromise.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
These teachings immediately made the great merchants of Quraysh feel that their material interests were under threat.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The worship of idols, many of which were gathered in the Kaʿba at Mecca, was one of their important sources of profit. It made Mecca a destination for tribes from at least the north-west and north-east of Arabia.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The pilgrimage seasons around the Kaʿba, where these idols were gathered, also concentrated some of the most profitable commercial and moneylending activity in Arabia. This activity strengthened the leading figures of the Meccan Dār al-Nadwa, the emerging form of “political” authority through which they exercised their commercial and financial power.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That was one side of the danger perceived by the Quraysh leadership.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The other came from the broader moral and humanitarian teachings of the early Islamic message.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

These teachings called for the material suffering of the lower social groups to be eased. They called for justice toward the poor, the weak, and the needy. They taught that people were equal in standing before God regardless of race, color, blood, or ancestry.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Other Qur’anic verses condemned usury, the monopolization of basic necessities, the hoarding of gold and silver, and similar practices.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Most of these Meccan teachings were moral rather than legal in character.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Even so, they gave the leaders of the Dār al-Nadwa the impression that Islam had arrived to place its full weight on the opposite side of the emerging balance of social forces in late pre-Islamic society, which we discussed in the previous chapter.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That opposite side was the side of the lower social groups: those being oppressed and exploited by the commercial and tribal leaders of the time.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

But this early and undeveloped class consciousness, expressed in the tense reaction against Islam, was historically unable to see that this opposition was not actually in the long-term interests of the Quraysh merchant leadership itself.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In fact, Muruwwa argues, the opposite was true.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

If that leadership had been able, during the early Meccan period, to see the historical direction in which Arab society was moving, and to see that Islam was moving in the same direction, it would have recognized that Islam was also opening the path to its own future development.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Quraysh merchants were already forming the nucleus of a class that was capable of playing a major role in the new social order that was about to emerge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It is enough here to say that Islam appeared at a historical moment when the tribal framework had reached the point where it had to break apart.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
A single unifying framework now had to replace it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Only such a framework could create the conditions needed for the rise of a genuinely new Arab society—not simply a larger collection of tribes, but a society different in quality, with new relations of production, a new social structure, and new institutions created to organize those relations and develop their material foundations.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But at the moment when Islam emerged, it was only beginning to take shape within the new historical horizon opened by the Islamic message.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

It is therefore correct to say that breaking apart the tribal frameworks and establishing a single unifying framework—the first major task of the historical stage opened by Islam—did not actually conflict with the interests of the very group that spent thirteen years fighting Islam with fierce hostility.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Without realizing it, the Quraysh leadership was delaying the beginning of its own development: its transformation into a major class that would later help build the Arab-Islamic society that followed.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This was the mistake in the Quraysh leadership’s view of its own “class” interests and their supposed conflict with Islam.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The direction of historical development was not toward the contradiction they imagined.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

On the contrary, the logic of that development eventually required what happened after the conquest of Mecca: the Quraysh leadership joined the historical transformations set in motion by Islam after its victory in Arabia and its expansion onto the wider world stage of the time.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
B — The Universe and the Human Being Within the Framework of Monotheism
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The historical need to break apart the tribal framework and replace it with a unifying one arose, in Muruwwa’s view, from the laws governing social development at that particular historical moment.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islamic monotheism was the central religious expression of the relationship between Islam and the social conditions of that particular time and place.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

But this relationship also appeared in other forms. The different institutions and teachings of Islam were connected in different ways to the particular historical features of the society in which Islam emerged.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
One of the most important of these was the intellectual dimension of monotheism.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This would have a deep effect on the later relationship between two processes: the development of Arab-Islamic society and the development of Arab-Islamic thought.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The interaction between these two processes would help create a common intellectual world whose roots lay in a common ground: Islam itself.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The intellectual dimension of monotheism began to appear in the earliest Islamic teachings.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
These teachings offered forms of knowledge about the universe, including knowledge of nature and of the human being’s place, role, and responsibilities within it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Everything Islam taught about these subjects through the language of the Qur’an served the central issue of the Islamic message: establishing monotheism as a religious belief and as the foundation of the ideological system that would later develop around it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Many of the Qur’anic verses revealed during the early Meccan period, before the great migration to Medina, were concerned with this intellectual dimension.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
They presented the “metaphysics” of Islam as a complete system centered on the idea of one God.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This divine unity gave the universe its unity and also gave human understanding of that universe a single organizing principle.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At the foundation of this system stood the idea of creation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The universe as a whole, and everything within it, was created by the one God, who has no partner.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In other words, the universe was created from “nothing.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This means that the world had a beginning. It was not eternal.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
If the world had a beginning, then matter, motion, time, and space also had beginnings. None of them is eternal.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And anything that is not eternal in the past is not everlasting in the future, because whatever has a beginning must also have an end.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
All created worlds therefore pass away.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
No person and no thing lives forever in this earthly life.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But the idea of immortality remains.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

If immortality does not belong to this life, then it belongs to what comes after death: the second life, where every person receives the result of what they did in the first. Good is answered with good, and evil with evil.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Our earthly world—the world of nature that we experience through our senses—is to be known from the divine source of knowledge, revelation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Its story is this: it existed first in the darkness of nonexistence. God created it. And it will return to the darkness of nonexistence, to annihilation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The natural world is neither eternal nor everlasting.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
God’s will is absolute in both its creation and its destruction.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The old theory of “coming-to-be and passing-away” therefore takes a particular form here in Islamic religious thought.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Things come into being from outside themselves, through God. Then the will of the Creator brings every created thing eventually to corruption and annihilation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In the source of his coming-to-be and passing-away, the human being is no different from other created things.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But his place among them is different.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The human being is the highest of created beings.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“The Qur’an made Adam’s creation from the substance of life a symbol of the appearance of the human being on earth and of his elevation above the angels.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And when We said to the angels, “Bow before Adam,” they bowed, except for Iblīs. He refused, acted proudly, and became one of the unbelievers. (Surat al-Baqara, verse 34)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Can we see in this Qur’anic human being—formed from the “substance of life” and placed above the angels—a clear sign of Islam’s grounding in earthly reality?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Let us look again at this Qur’anic picture of the human being:
The Period of the Rise of Islam

And when your Lord said to the angels: “I am creating a human being from dry clay, formed from dark mud. When I have shaped him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration.” Then all the angels prostrated together, except Iblīs, who refused to join those who prostrated. He said: “Iblīs, why are you not among those who prostrate?” He replied: “I would never prostrate before a human being whom You created from dry clay, formed from dark mud.” He said: “Then leave this place, for you are rejected.” (Surat al-Ḥijr, verses 28–34)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
When your Lord said to the angels: “I am creating a human being from clay.” (Surat Ṣād, verse 71)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
So the human being is made from earthly clay, formed from the substance of this earth.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And yet this earthly human being is worthy of receiving the prostration of the angels, who in Qur’anic language are spiritual beings.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This comparison, followed by the elevation of the human being above the angels, allows us to see an inner connection between Islam’s “metaphysical” world and its world of earthly reality.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The same connection also links monotheism as a purely religious belief with monotheism as a social framework for the world of human beings made from clay.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And through this hidden connection, the human world is tied to the unity of the universe as a whole.
